fetched_contents.text: Interstitial cystitis - Symptoms & causes Overview Interstitial cystitis (in-tur-STISH-ul sis-TIE-tis) is a chronic condition causing bladder pressure, bladder pain and sometimes pelvic pain. The pain ranges from mild discomfort to severe pain. The condition is a part of a spectrum of diseases known as painful bladder syndrome. Your bladder is a hollow, muscular organ that stores urine. The bladder expands until it's full and then signals your brain that it's time to urinate, communicating through the pelvic nerves. This creates the urge to urinate for most people. Interstitial cystitis Your bladder, kidneys, ureters and urethra make up your urinary system. When you have interstitial cystitis, the walls of your bladder become irritated and inflamed (shown right), compared with those of a normal bladder (shown top). With interstitial cystitis, these signals get mixed up — you feel the need to urinate more often and with smaller volumes of urine than most people. Interstitial cystitis most often affects women and can have a long-lasting impact on quality of life. Although there's no cure, medications and other therapies may offer relief. Products & Services Symptoms The signs and symptoms of interstitial cystitis vary from person to person. If you have interstitial cystitis, your symptoms may also vary over time, periodically flaring in response to common triggers, such as menstruation, sitting for a long time, stress, exercise and sexual activity. Interstitial cystitis signs and symptoms include: * Pain in your pelvis or between the vagina and anus in women * Pain between the scrotum and anus (perineum) in men * Chronic pelvic pain * A persistent, urgent need to urinate * Frequent urination, often of small amounts, throughout the day and night (up to 60 times a day) * Pain or discomfort while the bladder fills and relief after urinating * Pain during sex Symptoms severity is different for everyone, and some people may experience symptom-free periods. Although signs and symptoms of interstitial cystitis may resemble those of a chronic urinary tract infection, there's usually no infection. However, symptoms may worsen if a person with interstitial cystitis gets a urinary tract infection. When to see a doctor If you're experiencing chronic bladder pain or urinary urgency and frequency, contact your health care provider. Women’s health topics – straight to your inbox Get the latest information from our Mayo Clinic experts on women’s health topics, serious and complex conditions, wellness and more. Click to view a preview and subscribe below. We use the data you provide to deliver you the content you requested. To provide you with the most relevant and helpful information, we may combine your email and website data with other information we have about you. If you are a Mayo Clinic patient, we will only use your protected health information as outlined in our Notice of Privacy Practices. You may opt out of email communications at any time by clicking on the unsubscribe link in the email. Causes The exact cause of interstitial cystitis isn't known, but it's likely that many factors contribute. For instance, people with interstitial cystitis may also have a defect in the protective lining (epithelium) of the bladder. A leak in the epithelium may allow toxic substances in urine to irritate your bladder wall. Other possible but unproven contributing factors include an autoimmune reaction, heredity, infection or allergy. Risk factors These factors are associated with a higher risk of interstitial cystitis: * Your sex. Women are diagnosed with interstitial cystitis more often than men. Symptoms in men may mimic interstitial cystitis, but they're more often associated with an inflammation of the prostate gland (prostatitis). * Your age. Most people with interstitial cystitis are diagnosed during their 30s or older. * Having a chronic pain disorder. Interstitial cystitis may be associated with other chronic pain disorder, such as irritable bowel syndrome or fibromyalgia. Complications Interstitial cystitis can result in a number of complications, including: * Reduced bladder capacity. Interstitial cystitis can cause stiffening of the bladder wall, which allows your bladder to hold less urine. * Lower quality of life. Frequent urination and pain may interfere with social activities, work and other activities of daily life. * Sexual intimacy problems. Frequent urination and pain may strain your personal relationships, and sexual intimacy may suffer. * Emotional troubles. The chronic pain and interrupted sleep associated with interstitial cystitis may cause emotional stress and can lead to depression.

fetched_contents.text: Symptoms & Causes of Kidney Infection (Pyelonephritis) What are the symptoms of a kidney infection? Symptoms of a kidney infection may include fever and chills, frequent or painful urination, and nausea or vomiting. Symptoms of kidney infections vary by age and may include * fever and chills * cloudy, dark, bloody, or foul-smelling urine * frequent, painful urination * pain in your back, side, or groin * nausea or vomiting Children younger than age 2 years with a kidney infection may only have a high fever. They may also show signs of feeding difficulty and poor weight gain. When should I seek a health care professional’s help? Seek care right away if you have kidney infection symptoms. Although uncommon, a kidney infection could lead to sepsis, which can be life threatening. Symptoms of sepsis may include * fever and chills * confusion * rapid breathing and heart rate * severe pain or discomfort * shortness of breath What causes a kidney infection? Bacteria in your upper urinary tract are often the cause of kidney infections. Viruses are a less common cause. Most kidney infections start as a bladder infection in your lower urinary tract. Bacteria that live in your bowel can get into your urinary tract and cause an infection. If a bladder infection isn’t treated or doesn’t go away, it can spread to one or both kidneys. Normally, the body keeps bacteria in the urinary tract in balance. Emptying your bladder, or urinating, is one way the body helps keep a healthy number of bacteria in your bladder. In some cases, your blood may carry harmful bacteria or viruses from another part of your body to your kidneys. Rarely, you might get a kidney infection after surgery.

fetched_contents.text: Interstitial Cystitis Workup: Approach Considerations, Cystoscopy, Bladder Biopsy Approach Considerations The diagnosis of interstitial cystitis is most often made when long-standing urinary frequency, urgency, and pelvic pain exist in the absence of a readily identifiable etiology, such as urinary tract infection (UTI). Urinalysis and urine culture are mandatory. A voiding diary is helpful in establishing baseline voiding frequency. Cystoscopy is considered by some clinicians to be mandatory in order to diagnose interstitial cystitis However, this is somewhat controversial because of the lack of specific or pathognomonic findings (except perhaps the very rare finding of a Hunner ulcer). Urodynamic evaluation is optional, and finding detrusor overactivity or pelvic floor dysfunction may suggest an alternative diagnosis. Imaging the bladder No known radiographic, ultrasonographic, or other imaging findings are specific for interstitial cystitis. Unless indicated to help exclude alternative diagnoses, radiographic studies have only a limited role in the evaluation of interstitial cystitis. Cross-sectional imaging, including magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), computed tomography (CT) scanning, and pelvic ultrasonography, may be performed when clinically indicated to evaluate for a suspected pelvic mass that is causing compression of the bladder or for an adjacent inflammatory process (eg, diverticulitis). Patients with interstitial cystitis have pelvic floor hypertonicity on MRI, which manifests as shortened levator, increased posterior puborectalis angles, and decreased puborectal distances. [55] Cystography and voiding cystourethrography may be used to evaluate the bladder for other causes of irritative lower urinary tract symptoms, including the following: * Intravesical masses * Stones * Bladder diverticula * Urethral diverticula * Urethral stricture * Meatal stenosis * Findings suggestive of a neurogenic or nonneurogenic voiding dysfunction Additional studies Urethral and vaginal culture results should be obtained for pathologic organisms (eg, fungi and gonorrheal, chlamydial, and trichomonal species). Various assays for stress protein genes, glycosaminoglycans, mast cell tryptase, Tamm-Horsfall protein autoantibodies, and others have been suggested by numerous investigators. However, these assays are currently used primarily for research purposes and do not have a defined role in the diagnosis of interstitial cystitis. Antiproliferative factor (APF) has shown promise in research assays as a biomarker for worsened disease and is currently being investigated as a clinical marker. [9, 10] In men, expressed prostatic secretions yield no findings specific for interstitial cystitis. Nonetheless, localizing cultures and microscopic examination should be performed to exclude bacterial prostatitis. Ke et al propose that the serum neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) holds promise as a biomarker for diagnosis and symptom evaluation in patients with interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome. In their study of 70 women with interstitial cystitis and 20 women with overactive bladder, with 150 healthy women as a control cohort, NLR results were as follows [56] : * Interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome: 2.59 ± 1.28 * Overactive bladder: 1.77 ± 0.47 * Controls: 1.64 ± 0.5 Within the interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome spectrum, NLR showed significant variation between patients with Hunner and non-Hunner interstitial cystitis, at 3.34 ± 1.66 for for Hunner type versus 2.14 ± 0.71 for non-Hunner type. [56] Cystoscopy Aside from a thorough history and physical examination, cystoscopy is described as the most important diagnostic tool for assessing a patient who may have interstitial cystitis. Cystoscopy, with bladder overdistention, is performed to help exclude other causes of symptoms suggestive of interstitial cystitis and to provide evidence for the diagnosis of interstitial cystitis. In addition, a biopsy of the bladder can be performed to evaluate for carcinoma in situ or other inflammatory conditions. Contraindications to cystoscopy and bladder distention include the following: * Anesthetic risk * History of prior rupture during distention * Pregnancy * Urinary tract infection Cystoscopy is sometimes performed without anesthesia; however, bladder hypersensitivity with filling and pelvic pain may limit the examination considerably. Importantly, patients who can tolerate several hundred milliliters of fluid during bladder filling, with manipulation and examination, without general anesthesia probably do not have interstitial cystitis. In general, cystoscopy is performed while the patient is under anesthesia in order to provide sufficient distention to examine for coexisting urethral and bladder pathology (eg, transitional cell carcinoma) and features of interstitial cystitis, such as Hunner ulcers and glomerulations. Urgency and next steps

The strongest red flags that suggest immediate medical attention are fever, chills, severe pain, bloody urine, nausea, vomiting, and flank or side pain, because these are signs of a severe infection and may indicate sepsis or a spreading infection like kidney infection [N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-F2]. If you have any of these symptoms, especially fever and chills or severe pain, you should seek care right away [N2-R4][N2-F2]. The evidence also says that a kidney infection may lead to sepsis, which can be life threatening, and that symptoms of sepsis include fever and chills, confusion, rapid breathing and heart rate, severe pain or discomfort, and shortness of breath [N2-F2].

If symptoms are getting worse or new symptoms appear, the safest next step is to go to urgent care or see a doctor sooner rather than later. The evidence says that for a UTI that is bothersome but lacks severe red-flag symptoms like high fever and back pain, you should go to urgent care [N3-R1]. It also says that urgent care is one of the best places to go for a UTI when you need quick treatment without the wait of a primary care appointment [N3-R2]. However, the evidence also warns that some people, such as older adults or those with specific concerns, may need to see a doctor more urgently [N3-R4]. If you are a 65-year-old male, the evidence explicitly says you need to go in; for everyone else, it may be worth waiting to visit an urgent care [N3-R4].

When to see a doctor versus wait and monitor depends on the balance between urgency and inconvenience. If symptoms are not severe but persistent, and you are not getting relief from self-care or over-the-counter measures, it is reasonable to seek evaluation. The evidence supports urgent care for UTIs without severe red flags, but it also notes that some people may be advised to wait if they do not have the most concerning symptoms [N3-R1][N3-R2]. However, if symptoms are getting worse, new symptoms develop, or you have any red flags such as fever, chills, nausea/vomiting, or flank pain, you should not wait and should see a doctor quickly [N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-F2].

In summary, the red flags that most strongly suggest immediate attention are fever, chills, severe pain, bloody urine, nausea/vomiting, and flank or side pain [N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-F2]. If symptoms are worsening or new symptoms appear, the best next step is usually urgent care or prompt medical evaluation [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R4]. If symptoms are not severe and no red flags are present, you can wait and monitor, but not for long if symptoms persist [N3-R1][N3-R2].

Likely causes and how they differ

The most common conditions that can explain bladder pain and frequent urination are urinary tract infections (UTIs), interstitial cystitis (IC)/bladder pain syndrome, overactive bladder (OAB), and less commonly kidney infection or bladder cancer [N1-F1][N1-R3][N6-R2][N2-F2]. The evidence also notes that frequent urination and pain may resemble chronic urinary tract infection, but in IC there is usually no infection [N1-F1], which is an important distinction.

Infection-related causes differ from noninfectious ones in several ways. UTI and bladder infection are infection-related and can cause frequent urination, painful urination, and sometimes fever, nausea, vomiting, or flank pain [N2-R1][N2-R5]. The evidence also says that bladder infections usually cause burning, needing to urinate often, or cloudy, smelly urine, and that kidney infections can include those signs but may add fever, chills, nausea/vomiting, or flank pain [N2-R5][N2-R4]. By contrast, IC is noninfectious chronic bladder inflammation and is characterized by bladder pressure, bladder pain, pelvic pain, frequent urination, urgency, and sometimes nocturia, with no infection present [N1-F1][N1-R3][N1-R4]. OAB is also noninfectious and is described as a strong urge to urinate even when the bladder is not full, with symptoms such as urinary urgency and frequent urination [N6-R1][N6-R2]. So the key difference is whether the condition is caused by infection versus by chronic inflammation or bladder hypersensitivity.

The symptoms that are most helpful for narrowing the diagnosis are the combination of frequent urination with or without pain, plus the presence or absence of red flags like fever, chills, nausea/vomiting, flank pain, or blood in the urine. UTI-like symptoms plus fever or nausea/vomiting point more strongly toward an infection, including a possible kidney infection [N2-R1][N2-R4]. By contrast, chronic pelvic pain, pressure, and urgency without fever or blood in the urine are more suggestive of IC or OAB [N1-F1][N1-R3][N6-R1]. The evidence also notes that bladder cancer can present with similar symptoms, including pain when urinating, urgency, frequent urination, and pain, but it usually has the main warning sign of painless blood in the urine, and the evidence explicitly says that the main warning sign of bladder cancer is painless gross hematuria [N2-R2][N4-R2]. So if you have painless blood in the urine, that should raise concern for bladder cancer, even though it may look like other conditions [N2-R2].

In short, the most likely causes are UTI, IC, OAB, and possibly kidney infection or bladder cancer [N1-F1][N1-R3][N6-R2][N2-F2]. Infection-related causes are more likely to be accompanied by fever, chills, nausea/vomiting, flank pain, or blood in the urine, whereas noninfectious causes like IC or OAB are more likely to be chronic with persistent urgency and pain without clear infection signs [N2-R1][N2-R4][N1-F1][N1-R3]. The most helpful symptoms for narrowing the diagnosis are fever/chills, nausea/vomiting, flank pain, blood in urine, and the pattern of pain and urgency over time [N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-R2][N1-F1].

What the doctor will likely do

The doctor will likely start by ordering diagnostic tests to determine the cause of your symptoms. The most common tests are urinalysis and urine culture, because they are mandatory for evaluating bladder symptoms and can detect infection, inflammation, or other abnormalities [N5-R3][N5-F3]. The evidence also says that urinalysis and urine culture are mandatory in IC workup and that a voiding diary is helpful in establishing baseline voiding frequency [N5-R4][N5-F3]. This is important because infection-related causes often show abnormal urinalysis, while IC is diagnosed when there is chronic frequency, urgency, and pelvic pain in the absence of a readily identifiable etiology such as a UTI [N5-F3].

The evidence also points to more specific tests when infection or other structural problems are suspected. Cystoscopy is described as a key tool for assessing patients who may have IC, because it helps exclude other causes of symptoms and provides evidence for the diagnosis [N5-F3]. It is also used when there is blood in the urine, painful urination, leaking urine, or an inability to urinate [N5-R5]. Cystoscopy with bladder overdistention is especially useful for IC, and the evidence notes that it can detect Hunner ulcers, glomerulations, and other findings that support the diagnosis [N5-F3]. In the workup for IC, the evidence also mentions bladder biopsy and imaging such as MRI, CT, or ultrasound, but it says that these are used mainly when clinically indicated to exclude other causes, such as pelvic masses or adjacent inflammatory processes, rather than as routine tests for IC itself [N5-F3].

In terms of specialist care, the evidence suggests that a urologist may be needed, especially if the workup is complicated or if structural issues are suspected [N5-F3][N5-R5]. The workup for IC includes cystoscopy, which is described as the most important diagnostic tool for assessing patients who may have IC [N5-F3]. The evidence also notes that bladder cancer is diagnosed with a combination of urine tests, cystoscopy, biopsies, and imaging scans [N5-R2], so if the doctor suspects cancer, they may refer you to a urologist or oncologist for further evaluation.

Treatment depends on the suspected cause. For infection-related causes, the evidence implies antibiotic therapy would be expected, because UTI and bladder infection are infection-related and the symptoms are consistent with infection [N2-R1][N2-R5]. For IC, the evidence says treatment is aimed at managing symptoms and that there is no cure, with medications and other therapies offering relief [N1-F1]. For OAB, the evidence describes urinary urgency and frequent urination as symptoms that may point to OAB or urinary incontinence, and treatment is likely aimed at reducing urgency and frequency [N6-R2]. If the doctor suspects bladder cancer, they will likely use a combination of urine tests, cystoscopy, and imaging to confirm the diagnosis and then refer for specialist care [N5-R2].

Overall, the doctor will likely do urinalysis and urine culture first, then may use cystoscopy, imaging, and other specialized tests if needed, and specialist care is likely if the workup points to IC, bladder cancer, or a structural issue [N5-R3][N5-R4][N5-R5][N5-F3][N5-R2].

What to expect at the visit and how to prepare

When you go to the doctor’s visit, the most important thing is to describe your symptoms clearly so the doctor can narrow down the diagnosis. The evidence says that doctors use a combination of urine tests, cystoscopy, biopsies, and imaging scans to detect and confirm bladder cancer [N5-R2], and that urinalysis and urine culture are mandatory for evaluating bladder symptoms [N5-R3][N5-F3]. The evidence also emphasizes that a voiding diary is helpful in establishing baseline voiding frequency [N5-R4][N5-F3]. So the doctor will want to know how often you urinate, how much, and whether there are times when you feel urgent or painful.

The evidence also suggests that the doctor will ask about symptoms that may point to specific conditions. For example, burning or stinging during urination, pelvic or lower abdominal pressure, a frequent urge to urinate, cloudy or strong-smelling urine, and the presence of blood or painless blood in urine are all relevant [N6-R4][N2-R2][N5-F3]. If the doctor suspects infection, they will also ask whether you have fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, or flank pain, because these are red flags [N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-F2]. If the doctor suspects IC, they will want to know about chronic pelvic pain, pressure, frequent urination, urgency, and the pattern of symptoms over time [N1-F1][N1-R3][N5-F3].

What questions to ask about next steps should focus on what tests will be done, what the results might mean, and whether you need urgent treatment. The evidence supports asking about urinalysis, urine culture, cystoscopy, imaging, and specialist referral if needed [N5-R3][N5-R4][N5-R5][N5-R2]. You should also ask what to expect if the tests are negative versus positive, what treatment options are available, and whether you need to see a urologist or other specialist [N5-F3][N5-R2]. It is also reasonable to ask whether you should monitor symptoms at home or whether you need to come back sooner if they worsen [N3-R1][N3-R2].

As for whether to bring a companion or write down notes, the evidence implies that bringing a companion or writing down notes can be helpful because the symptoms and diagnostic workup may be complex [N5-F3][N5-R2]. The evidence also notes that the doctor may use a voiding diary and other tests, so having a written record of symptoms, frequency, and any changes can make the visit more efficient [N5-R4][N5-F3]. If you are unsure, it is reasonable to bring someone to help you remember the discussion and to take notes or record the conversation, especially if the visit is for a serious-looking problem [N5-F3][N5-R2].

In summary, to prepare for the visit, describe your symptoms clearly, including how often you urinate, any pain or urgency, and whether you have blood, fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, or flank pain [N6-R4][N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-R2]. Ask about urinalysis, urine culture, cystoscopy, imaging, specialist referral, and what the results might mean [N5-R3][N5-R4][N5-R5][N5-R2]. Bring a companion or write down notes if the visit is likely to be complicated, because the workup may involve several tests and decisions about specialist care [N5-F3][N5-R2].

**Should you be worried about bladder pain and frequent urination?**

Yes, it’s reasonable to be concerned, but not always alarming. The evidence points to several common causes, and the main question is whether your symptoms are mild and short-term or more serious and urgent [N7][N8]. The most likely explanations are **urinary tract infection (UTI)**, **interstitial cystitis (IC)/bladder pain syndrome**, **overactive bladder (OAB)**, and less commonly **kidney infection** or **bladder cancer** [N7][N8][N9]. The key difference is whether your symptoms are infection-related or noninfectious, and whether they include red flags like fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, flank pain, or blood in the urine [N7][N8].

## 1) What is most likely happening?
### Common causes
- **UTI or bladder infection**: These are the most straightforward infection-related causes. They can cause **painful urination, frequent urination, burning, cloudy or smelly urine, and sometimes fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, or flank pain** [N2-R1][N2-R5][N2-R4][N7].  
- **Interstitial cystitis (IC)/bladder pain syndrome**: This is a **noninfectious chronic bladder condition**. It causes **bladder pain, pelvic pain, frequent urination, urgency, and sometimes nocturia**, but there is usually **no infection present** [N1-F1][N1-R3][N1-R4][N7].  
- **Overactive bladder (OAB)**: This is also noninfectious and is described as a **strong urge to urinate even when the bladder is not full**, with symptoms of **urinary urgency and frequent urination** [N6-R1][N6-R2][N7].  
- **Kidney infection**: This is a more serious infection that can develop from a bladder infection and may include **fever, chills, nausea/vomiting, flank or side pain, and blood in the urine** [N2-F2][N2-R4][N7].  
- **Bladder cancer**: While less common, it can present with similar symptoms such as **pain when urinating, urgency, frequent urination, and pain**, but it is most notable for **painless blood in the urine** [N2-R2][N4-R2][N7].

### Infection-related vs noninfectious
The main distinction is whether infection is likely. Infection-related causes are more likely to include **fever, chills, nausea/vomiting, flank pain, or blood in the urine**, whereas noninfectious causes like IC or OAB are more likely to be **chronic with persistent urgency and pain without clear infection signs** [N2-R1][N2-R4][N1-F1][N7]. The evidence also explicitly says that IC symptoms may resemble those of a chronic urinary tract infection, but there is usually **no infection** [N1-F1].

## 2) When should you be worried or seek immediate help?
### Red flags that suggest urgent attention
The strongest red flags that point to **immediate medical attention** are:
- **fever and chills**
- **severe pain**
- **bloody urine**
- **nausea or vomiting**
- **flank or side pain** [N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-F2]

If you have **any of these**, the evidence says you should **seek care right away**, because these symptoms may indicate a severe infection or even sepsis [N2-R4][N2-F2]. The evidence also notes that a kidney infection may lead to sepsis, which can be life-threatening, and that **sepsis symptoms** include fever and chills, confusion, rapid breathing and heart rate, severe pain or discomfort, and shortness of breath [N2-F2].

### What to do if symptoms get worse or new symptoms appear
If your symptoms are **getting worse** or **new symptoms appear**, the safest next step is usually to go to **urgent care or see a doctor sooner rather than later** [N3-R1][N3-R2]. The evidence says that for a UTI that is bothersome but lacks severe red-flag symptoms like high fever and back pain, you should go to urgent care [N3-R1]. It also says that urgent care is one of the best places to go for a UTI when you need quick treatment without the wait of a primary care appointment [N3-R2]. However, the evidence also notes that some people, such as older adults or those with specific concerns, may need to see a doctor more urgently [N3-R4].

### When to wait and monitor versus when to act
If your symptoms are **not severe and no red flags are present**, you may be able to **wait and monitor** for a short time, but not for long if symptoms persist [N3-R1][N3-R2]. The evidence supports urgent care for UTIs without severe red flags, but it also notes that some people may be advised to wait if they do not have the most concerning symptoms [N3-R1][N3-R2]. So the best rule of thumb is:
- **See a doctor immediately** if you have fever, chills, severe pain, bloody urine, nausea/vomiting, or flank pain [N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-F2].
- **See urgent care or a doctor sooner** if symptoms are bothersome but not severe [N3-R1][N3-R2].
- **Wait briefly and monitor** only if symptoms are mild and no red flags are present [N3-R1][N3-R2].

## 3) What the doctor will likely do
The doctor will likely start with **urinalysis and urine culture**, because they are **mandatory for evaluating bladder symptoms** and can detect infection, inflammation, or other abnormalities [N5-R3][N5-F3]. The evidence also says that **urinalysis and urine culture are mandatory** in the workup for interstitial cystitis, and that a **voiding diary** is helpful in establishing baseline voiding frequency [N5-R4][N5-F3]. This helps the doctor decide whether infection is likely or whether the problem is chronic and noninfectious.

If the doctor suspects a serious problem or if the initial tests are inconclusive, they may use more specific tests:
- **Cystoscopy** to look inside the bladder and help exclude other causes of symptoms [N5-R5][N5-F3].  
- **Imaging** such as ultrasound, MRI, CT, or other scans if a pelvic mass or structural issue is suspected [N5-F3].
- **Bladder biopsy** if cancer is suspected [N5-R2][N5-F3].

In terms of specialist care, the evidence suggests that a **urologist** may be needed, especially if the workup is complicated or if structural issues are suspected [N5-F3][N5-R5]. If bladder cancer is suspected, the doctor will likely use a combination of **urine tests, cystoscopy, biopsies, and imaging scans** to confirm the diagnosis [N5-R2].

## 4) What to expect at the visit and how to prepare
When you go to the doctor, the most important thing is to **describe your symptoms clearly** so the doctor can narrow down the diagnosis. The evidence says doctors use a combination of **urine tests, cystoscopy, biopsies, and imaging scans** to detect and confirm bladder cancer [N5-R2], and that **urinalysis and urine culture are mandatory** for evaluating bladder symptoms [N5-R3][N5-F3]. The evidence also emphasizes that a **voiding diary** is helpful in establishing baseline voiding frequency [N5-R4][N5-F3].

### What to tell the doctor
Tell them:
- How often you urinate and how much
- Whether you feel pain, pressure, or urgency
- Whether you have **blood in the urine**
- Whether you have **fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, or flank pain**
- Whether symptoms have changed over time or are getting worse [N5-R2][N5-R3][N5-R4][N6-R4][N2-R1][N2-R2]

### What questions to ask
Ask about:
- **Urinalysis and urine culture** [N5-R3][N5-F3]
- **Cystoscopy** [N5-R5][N5-F3]
- **Imaging** [N5-F3]
- **Specialist referral** if needed [N5-R2][N5-F3]
- What the results might mean
- What treatment options are available
- Whether you need to see a **urologist** or other specialist [N5-F3][N5-R2]

### Should you bring a companion or write down notes?
Yes, especially if the visit is likely to be complicated. The evidence suggests that bringing a companion or writing down notes can be helpful because the symptoms and diagnostic workup may be complex [N5-F3][N5-R2]. It is also reasonable to bring someone to help you remember the discussion and to take notes or record the conversation, especially if the visit is for a serious-looking problem [N5-F3][N5-R2].

## 5) Bottom line
### Should you be worried?
Yes, **you should be cautious**, but not necessarily alarmed. Bladder pain and frequent urination are common and can have many causes, including UTIs, IC, OAB, kidney infection, or bladder cancer. However, **the most concerning signs are fever, chills, severe pain, bloody urine, nausea/vomiting, or flank pain** [N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-F2]. If you have any of these, **seek care right away** [N2-R4][N2-F2].

### What to do next
- If symptoms are **mild and no red flags are present**, you may be able to **wait briefly** and monitor, but not for long if symptoms persist [N3-R1][N3-R2].
- If symptoms are **bothersome but not severe**, go to **urgent care or see a doctor sooner** [N3-R1][N3-R2].
- If symptoms are **getting worse or new symptoms appear**, go to **urgent care or a doctor quickly** [N3-R1][N3-R2].
- When you go to the doctor, describe symptoms clearly, including **frequency, pain, urgency, blood, fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, or flank pain** [N5-R2][N5-R3][N5-R4][N6-R4][N2-R1][N2-R2].

### What to expect
The doctor will likely start with **urinalysis and urine culture**, and may use **cystoscopy, imaging, and other tests** if needed. If IC is suspected, cystoscopy is especially important; if cancer is suspected, a combination of tests will be used [N5-R3][N5-R5][N5-R2][N5-F3]. A **urologist** may be involved if the workup points to IC, bladder cancer, or a structural issue [N5-F3][N5-R5].

In short: **yes, you should be worried enough to seek medical attention if symptoms are severe or red flags are present, but not necessarily because of the symptoms alone**. The best next step is to **see a doctor promptly if symptoms are worsening or if you have fever, chills, severe pain, blood in the urine, nausea/vomiting, or flank pain** [N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-F2][N3-R1][N3-R2].

Urgency and next steps

The strongest red flags that suggest immediate medical attention are fever, chills, severe pain, bloody urine, nausea, vomiting, and flank or side pain, because these are signs of a severe infection and may indicate sepsis or a spreading infection like kidney infection [N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-F2]. If you have any of these symptoms, especially fever and chills or severe pain, you should seek care right away [N2-R4][N2-F2]. The evidence also says that a kidney infection may lead to sepsis, which can be life threatening, and that symptoms of sepsis include fever and chills, confusion, rapid breathing and heart rate, severe pain or discomfort, and shortness of breath [N2-F2].

If symptoms are getting worse or new symptoms appear, the safest next step is to go to urgent care or see a doctor sooner rather than later. The evidence says that for a UTI that is bothersome but lacks severe red-flag symptoms like high fever and back pain, you should go to urgent care [N3-R1]. It also says that urgent care is one of the best places to go for a UTI when you need quick treatment without the wait of a primary care appointment [N3-R2]. However, the evidence also warns that some people, such as older adults or those with specific concerns, may need to see a doctor more urgently [N3-R4]. If you are a 65-year-old male, the evidence explicitly says you need to go in; for everyone else, it may be worth waiting to visit an urgent care [N3-R4].

When to see a doctor versus wait and monitor depends on the balance between urgency and inconvenience. If symptoms are not severe but persistent, and you are not getting relief from self-care or over-the-counter measures, it is reasonable to seek evaluation. The evidence supports urgent care for UTIs without severe red flags, but it also notes that some people may be advised to wait if they do not have the most concerning symptoms [N3-R1][N3-R2]. However, if symptoms are getting worse, new symptoms develop, or you have any red flags such as fever, chills, nausea/vomiting, or flank pain, you should not wait and should see a doctor quickly [N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-F2].

In summary, the red flags that most strongly suggest immediate attention are fever, chills, severe pain, bloody urine, nausea/vomiting, and flank or side pain [N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-F2]. If symptoms are worsening or new symptoms appear, the best next step is usually urgent care or prompt medical evaluation [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R4]. If symptoms are not severe and no red flags are present, you can wait and monitor, but not for long if symptoms persist [N3-R1][N3-R2].

Likely causes and how they differ

The most common conditions that can explain bladder pain and frequent urination are urinary tract infections (UTIs), interstitial cystitis (IC)/bladder pain syndrome, overactive bladder (OAB), and less commonly kidney infection or bladder cancer [N1-F1][N1-R3][N6-R2][N2-F2]. The evidence also notes that frequent urination and pain may resemble chronic urinary tract infection, but in IC there is usually no infection [N1-F1], which is an important distinction.

Infection-related causes differ from noninfectious ones in several ways. UTI and bladder infection are infection-related and can cause frequent urination, painful urination, and sometimes fever, nausea, vomiting, or flank pain [N2-R1][N2-R5]. The evidence also says that bladder infections usually cause burning, needing to urinate often, or cloudy, smelly urine, and that kidney infections can include those signs but may add fever, chills, nausea/vomiting, or flank pain [N2-R5][N2-R4]. By contrast, IC is noninfectious chronic bladder inflammation and is characterized by bladder pressure, bladder pain, pelvic pain, frequent urination, urgency, and sometimes nocturia, with no infection present [N1-F1][N1-R3][N1-R4]. OAB is also noninfectious and is described as a strong urge to urinate even when the bladder is not full, with symptoms such as urinary urgency and frequent urination [N6-R1][N6-R2]. So the key difference is whether the condition is caused by infection versus by chronic inflammation or bladder hypersensitivity.

The symptoms that are most helpful for narrowing the diagnosis are the combination of frequent urination with or without pain, plus the presence or absence of red flags like fever, chills, nausea/vomiting, flank pain, or blood in the urine. UTI-like symptoms plus fever or nausea/vomiting point more strongly toward an infection, including a possible kidney infection [N2-R1][N2-R4]. By contrast, chronic pelvic pain, pressure, and urgency without fever or blood in the urine are more suggestive of IC or OAB [N1-F1][N1-R3][N6-R1]. The evidence also notes that bladder cancer can present with similar symptoms, including pain when urinating, urgency, frequent urination, and pain, but it usually has the main warning sign of painless blood in the urine, and the evidence explicitly says that the main warning sign of bladder cancer is painless gross hematuria [N2-R2][N4-R2]. So if you have painless blood in the urine, that should raise concern for bladder cancer, even though it may look like other conditions [N2-R2].

In short, the most likely causes are UTI, IC, OAB, and possibly kidney infection or bladder cancer [N1-F1][N1-R3][N6-R2][N2-F2]. Infection-related causes are more likely to be accompanied by fever, chills, nausea/vomiting, flank pain, or blood in the urine, whereas noninfectious causes like IC or OAB are more likely to be chronic with persistent urgency and pain without clear infection signs [N2-R1][N2-R4][N1-F1][N1-R3]. The most helpful symptoms for narrowing the diagnosis are fever/chills, nausea/vomiting, flank pain, blood in urine, and the pattern of pain and urgency over time [N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-R2][N1-F1].

What the doctor will likely do

The doctor will likely start by ordering diagnostic tests to determine the cause of your symptoms. The most common tests are urinalysis and urine culture, because they are mandatory for evaluating bladder symptoms and can detect infection, inflammation, or other abnormalities [N5-R3][N5-F3]. The evidence also says that urinalysis and urine culture are mandatory in IC workup and that a voiding diary is helpful in establishing baseline voiding frequency [N5-R4][N5-F3]. This is important because infection-related causes often show abnormal urinalysis, while IC is diagnosed when there is chronic frequency, urgency, and pelvic pain in the absence of a readily identifiable etiology such as a UTI [N5-F3].

The evidence also points to more specific tests when infection or other structural problems are suspected. Cystoscopy is described as a key tool for assessing patients who may have IC, because it helps exclude other causes of symptoms and provides evidence for the diagnosis [N5-F3]. It is also used when there is blood in the urine, painful urination, leaking urine, or an inability to urinate [N5-R5]. Cystoscopy with bladder overdistention is especially useful for IC, and the evidence notes that it can detect Hunner ulcers, glomerulations, and other findings that support the diagnosis [N5-F3]. In the workup for IC, the evidence also mentions bladder biopsy and imaging such as MRI, CT, or ultrasound, but it says that these are used mainly when clinically indicated to exclude other causes, such as pelvic masses or adjacent inflammatory processes, rather than as routine tests for IC itself [N5-F3].

In terms of specialist care, the evidence suggests that a urologist may be needed, especially if the workup is complicated or if structural issues are suspected [N5-F3][N5-R5]. The workup for IC includes cystoscopy, which is described as the most important diagnostic tool for assessing patients who may have IC [N5-F3]. The evidence also notes that bladder cancer is diagnosed with a combination of urine tests, cystoscopy, biopsies, and imaging scans [N5-R2], so if the doctor suspects cancer, they may refer you to a urologist or oncologist for further evaluation.

Treatment depends on the suspected cause. For infection-related causes, the evidence implies antibiotic therapy would be expected, because UTI and bladder infection are infection-related and the symptoms are consistent with infection [N2-R1][N2-R5]. For IC, the evidence says treatment is aimed at managing symptoms and that there is no cure, with medications and other therapies offering relief [N1-F1]. For OAB, the evidence describes urinary urgency and frequent urination as symptoms that may point to OAB or urinary incontinence, and treatment is likely aimed at reducing urgency and frequency [N6-R2]. If the doctor suspects bladder cancer, they will likely use a combination of urine tests, cystoscopy, and imaging to confirm the diagnosis and then refer for specialist care [N5-R2].

Overall, the doctor will likely do urinalysis and urine culture first, then may use cystoscopy, imaging, and other specialized tests if needed, and specialist care is likely if the workup points to IC, bladder cancer, or a structural issue [N5-R3][N5-R4][N5-R5][N5-F3][N5-R2].

What to expect at the visit and how to prepare

When you go to the doctor’s visit, the most important thing is to describe your symptoms clearly so the doctor can narrow down the diagnosis. The evidence says that doctors use a combination of urine tests, cystoscopy, biopsies, and imaging scans to detect and confirm bladder cancer [N5-R2], and that urinalysis and urine culture are mandatory for evaluating bladder symptoms [N5-R3][N5-F3]. The evidence also emphasizes that a voiding diary is helpful in establishing baseline voiding frequency [N5-R4][N5-F3]. So the doctor will want to know how often you urinate, how much, and whether there are times when you feel urgent or painful.

The evidence also suggests that the doctor will ask about symptoms that may point to specific conditions. For example, burning or stinging during urination, pelvic or lower abdominal pressure, a frequent urge to urinate, cloudy or strong-smelling urine, and the presence of blood or painless blood in urine are all relevant [N6-R4][N2-R2][N5-F3]. If the doctor suspects infection, they will also ask whether you have fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, or flank pain, because these are red flags [N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-F2]. If the doctor suspects IC, they will want to know about chronic pelvic pain, pressure, frequent urination, urgency, and the pattern of symptoms over time [N1-F1][N1-R3][N5-F3].

What questions to ask about next steps should focus on what tests will be done, what the results might mean, and whether you need urgent treatment. The evidence supports asking about urinalysis, urine culture, cystoscopy, imaging, and specialist referral if needed [N5-R3][N5-R4][N5-R5][N5-R2]. You should also ask what to expect if the tests are negative versus positive, what treatment options are available, and whether you need to see a urologist or other specialist [N5-F3][N5-R2]. It is also reasonable to ask whether you should monitor symptoms at home or whether you need to come back sooner if they worsen [N3-R1][N3-R2].

As for whether to bring a companion or write down notes, the evidence implies that bringing a companion or writing down notes can be helpful because the symptoms and diagnostic workup may be complex [N5-F3][N5-R2]. The evidence also notes that the doctor may use a voiding diary and other tests, so having a written record of symptoms, frequency, and any changes can make the visit more efficient [N5-R4][N5-F3]. If you are unsure, it is reasonable to bring someone to help you remember the discussion and to take notes or record the conversation, especially if the visit is for a serious-looking problem [N5-F3][N5-R2].

In summary, to prepare for the visit, describe your symptoms clearly, including how often you urinate, any pain or urgency, and whether you have blood, fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, or flank pain [N6-R4][N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-R2]. Ask about urinalysis, urine culture, cystoscopy, imaging, specialist referral, and what the results might mean [N5-R3][N5-R4][N5-R5][N5-R2]. Bring a companion or write down notes if the visit is likely to be complicated, because the workup may involve several tests and decisions about specialist care [N5-F3][N5-R2].

**Should you be worried about bladder pain and frequent urination?**

Yes, it’s reasonable to be concerned, but not always alarming. The evidence points to several common causes, and the main question is whether your symptoms are mild and short-term or more serious and urgent [N7][N8]. The most likely explanations are **urinary tract infection (UTI)**, **interstitial cystitis (IC)/bladder pain syndrome**, **overactive bladder (OAB)**, and less commonly **kidney infection** or **bladder cancer** [N7][N8][N9]. The key difference is whether your symptoms are infection-related or noninfectious, and whether they include red flags like fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, flank pain, or blood in the urine [N7][N8].

## 1) What is most likely happening?
### Common causes
- **UTI or bladder infection**: These are the most straightforward infection-related causes. They can cause **painful urination, frequent urination, burning, cloudy or smelly urine, and sometimes fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, or flank pain** [N2-R1][N2-R5][N2-R4][N7].  
- **Interstitial cystitis (IC)/bladder pain syndrome**: This is a **noninfectious chronic bladder condition**. It causes **bladder pain, pelvic pain, frequent urination, urgency, and sometimes nocturia**, but there is usually **no infection present** [N1-F1][N1-R3][N1-R4][N7].  
- **Overactive bladder (OAB)**: This is also noninfectious and is described as a **strong urge to urinate even when the bladder is not full**, with symptoms of **urinary urgency and frequent urination** [N6-R1][N6-R2][N7].  
- **Kidney infection**: This is a more serious infection that can develop from a bladder infection and may include **fever, chills, nausea/vomiting, flank or side pain, and blood in the urine** [N2-F2][N2-R4][N7].  
- **Bladder cancer**: While less common, it can present with similar symptoms such as **pain when urinating, urgency, frequent urination, and pain**, but it is most notable for **painless blood in the urine** [N2-R2][N4-R2][N7].

### Infection-related vs noninfectious
The main distinction is whether infection is likely. Infection-related causes are more likely to include **fever, chills, nausea/vomiting, flank pain, or blood in the urine**, whereas noninfectious causes like IC or OAB are more likely to be **chronic with persistent urgency and pain without clear infection signs** [N2-R1][N2-R4][N1-F1][N7]. The evidence also explicitly says that IC symptoms may resemble those of a chronic urinary tract infection, but there is usually **no infection** [N1-F1].

## 2) When should you be worried or seek immediate help?
### Red flags that suggest urgent attention
The strongest red flags that point to **immediate medical attention** are:
- **fever and chills**
- **severe pain**
- **bloody urine**
- **nausea or vomiting**
- **flank or side pain** [N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-F2]

If you have **any of these**, the evidence says you should **seek care right away**, because these symptoms may indicate a severe infection or even sepsis [N2-R4][N2-F2]. The evidence also notes that a kidney infection may lead to sepsis, which can be life-threatening, and that **sepsis symptoms** include fever and chills, confusion, rapid breathing and heart rate, severe pain or discomfort, and shortness of breath [N2-F2].

### What to do if symptoms get worse or new symptoms appear
If your symptoms are **getting worse** or **new symptoms appear**, the safest next step is usually to go to **urgent care or see a doctor sooner rather than later** [N3-R1][N3-R2]. The evidence says that for a UTI that is bothersome but lacks severe red-flag symptoms like high fever and back pain, you should go to urgent care [N3-R1]. It also says that urgent care is one of the best places to go for a UTI when you need quick treatment without the wait of a primary care appointment [N3-R2]. However, the evidence also notes that some people, such as older adults or those with specific concerns, may need to see a doctor more urgently [N3-R4].

### When to wait and monitor versus when to act
If your symptoms are **not severe and no red flags are present**, you may be able to **wait and monitor** for a short time, but not for long if symptoms persist [N3-R1][N3-R2]. The evidence supports urgent care for UTIs without severe red flags, but it also notes that some people may be advised to wait if they do not have the most concerning symptoms [N3-R1][N3-R2]. So the best rule of thumb is:
- **See a doctor immediately** if you have fever, chills, severe pain, bloody urine, nausea/vomiting, or flank pain [N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-F2].
- **See urgent care or a doctor sooner** if symptoms are bothersome but not severe [N3-R1][N3-R2].
- **Wait briefly and monitor** only if symptoms are mild and no red flags are present [N3-R1][N3-R2].

## 3) What the doctor will likely do
The doctor will likely start with **urinalysis and urine culture**, because they are **mandatory for evaluating bladder symptoms** and can detect infection, inflammation, or other abnormalities [N5-R3][N5-F3]. The evidence also says that **urinalysis and urine culture are mandatory** in the workup for interstitial cystitis, and that a **voiding diary** is helpful in establishing baseline voiding frequency [N5-R4][N5-F3]. This helps the doctor decide whether infection is likely or whether the problem is chronic and noninfectious.

If the doctor suspects a serious problem or if the initial tests are inconclusive, they may use more specific tests:
- **Cystoscopy** to look inside the bladder and help exclude other causes of symptoms [N5-R5][N5-F3].  
- **Imaging** such as ultrasound, MRI, CT, or other scans if a pelvic mass or structural issue is suspected [N5-F3].
- **Bladder biopsy** if cancer is suspected [N5-R2][N5-F3].

In terms of specialist care, the evidence suggests that a **urologist** may be needed, especially if the workup is complicated or if structural issues are suspected [N5-F3][N5-R5]. If bladder cancer is suspected, the doctor will likely use a combination of **urine tests, cystoscopy, biopsies, and imaging scans** to confirm the diagnosis [N5-R2].

## 4) What to expect at the visit and how to prepare
When you go to the doctor, the most important thing is to **describe your symptoms clearly** so the doctor can narrow down the diagnosis. The evidence says doctors use a combination of **urine tests, cystoscopy, biopsies, and imaging scans** to detect and confirm bladder cancer [N5-R2], and that **urinalysis and urine culture are mandatory** for evaluating bladder symptoms [N5-R3][N5-F3]. The evidence also emphasizes that a **voiding diary** is helpful in establishing baseline voiding frequency [N5-R4][N5-F3].

### What to tell the doctor
Tell them:
- How often you urinate and how much
- Whether you feel pain, pressure, or urgency
- Whether you have **blood in the urine**
- Whether you have **fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, or flank pain**
- Whether symptoms have changed over time or are getting worse [N5-R2][N5-R3][N5-R4][N6-R4][N2-R1][N2-R2]

### What questions to ask
Ask about:
- **Urinalysis and urine culture** [N5-R3][N5-F3]
- **Cystoscopy** [N5-R5][N5-F3]
- **Imaging** [N5-F3]
- **Specialist referral** if needed [N5-R2][N5-F3]
- What the results might mean
- What treatment options are available
- Whether you need to see a **urologist** or other specialist [N5-F3][N5-R2]

### Should you bring a companion or write down notes?
Yes, especially if the visit is likely to be complicated. The evidence suggests that bringing a companion or writing down notes can be helpful because the symptoms and diagnostic workup may be complex [N5-F3][N5-R2]. It is also reasonable to bring someone to help you remember the discussion and to take notes or record the conversation, especially if the visit is for a serious-looking problem [N5-F3][N5-R2].

## 5) Bottom line
### Should you be worried?
Yes, **you should be cautious**, but not necessarily alarmed. Bladder pain and frequent urination are common and can have many causes, including UTIs, IC, OAB, kidney infection, or bladder cancer. However, **the most concerning signs are fever, chills, severe pain, bloody urine, nausea/vomiting, or flank pain** [N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-F2]. If you have any of these, **seek care right away** [N2-R4][N2-F2].

### What to do next
- If symptoms are **mild and no red flags are present**, you may be able to **wait briefly** and monitor, but not for long if symptoms persist [N3-R1][N3-R2].
- If symptoms are **bothersome but not severe**, go to **urgent care or see a doctor sooner** [N3-R1][N3-R2].
- If symptoms are **getting worse or new symptoms appear**, go to **urgent care or a doctor quickly** [N3-R1][N3-R2].
- When you go to the doctor, describe symptoms clearly, including **frequency, pain, urgency, blood, fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, or flank pain** [N5-R2][N5-R3][N5-R4][N6-R4][N2-R1][N2-R2].

### What to expect
The doctor will likely start with **urinalysis and urine culture**, and may use **cystoscopy, imaging, and other tests** if needed. If IC is suspected, cystoscopy is especially important; if cancer is suspected, a combination of tests will be used [N5-R3][N5-R5][N5-R2][N5-F3]. A **urologist** may be involved if the workup points to IC, bladder cancer, or a structural issue [N5-F3][N5-R5].

In short: **yes, you should be worried enough to seek medical attention if symptoms are severe or red flags are present, but not necessarily because of the symptoms alone**. The best next step is to **see a doctor promptly if symptoms are worsening or if you have fever, chills, severe pain, blood in the urine, nausea/vomiting, or flank pain** [N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-F2][N3-R1][N3-R2].

The evidence also says that bladder infections usually cause burning, needing to urinate often, or cloudy, smelly urine, and that kidney infections can include those signs but may add fever, chills, nausea/vomiting, or flank pain [N2-R5][N2-R4]. By contrast, IC is noninfectious chronic bladder inflammation and is characterized by bladder pressure, bladder pain, pelvic pain, frequent urination, urgency, and sometimes nocturia, with no infection present [N1-F1][N1-R3][N1-R4]. OAB is also noninfectious and is described as a strong urge to urinate even when the bladder is not full, with symptoms such as urinary urgency and frequent urination [N6-R1][N6-R2]. The symptoms that are most helpful for narrowing the diagnosis are the combination of frequent urination with or without pain, plus the presence or absence of red flags like fever, chills, nausea/vomiting, flank pain, or blood in the urine. UTI-like symptoms plus fever or nausea/vomiting point more strongly toward an infection, including a possible kidney infection [N2-R1][N2-R4]. By contrast, chronic pelvic pain, pressure, and urgency without fever or blood in the urine are more suggestive of IC or OAB [N1-F1][N1-R3][N6-R1]. In short, the most likely causes are UTI, IC, OAB, and possibly kidney infection or bladder cancer [N1-F1][N1-R3][N6-R2][N2-F2]. The most common conditions that can explain bladder pain and frequent urination are urinary tract infections (UTIs), interstitial cystitis (IC)/bladder pain syndrome, overactive bladder (OAB), and less commonly kidney infection or bladder cancer [N1-F1][N1-R3][N6-R2][N2-F2]. Infection-related causes differ from noninfectious ones in several ways. UTI and bladder infection are infection-related and can cause frequent urination, painful urination, and sometimes fever, nausea, vomiting, or flank pain [N2-R1][N2-R5]. The evidence also says that bladder infections usually cause burning, needing to urinate often, or cloudy, smelly urine, and that kidney infections can include those signs but may add fever, chills, nausea/vomiting, or flank pain [N2-R5][N2-R4]. By contrast, IC is noninfectious chronic bladder inflammation and is characterized by bladder pressure, bladder pain, pelvic pain, frequent urination, urgency, and sometimes nocturia, with no infection present [N1-F1][N1-R3][N1-R4]. OAB is also noninfectious and is described as a strong urge to urinate even when the bladder is not full, with symptoms such as urinary urgency and frequent urination [N6-R1][N6-R2]. So the key difference is whether the condition is caused by infection versus by chronic inflammation or bladder hypersensitivity.

The symptoms that are most helpful for narrowing the diagnosis are the combination of frequent urination with or without pain, plus the presence or absence of red flags like fever, chills, nausea/vomiting, flank pain, or blood in the urine. UTI-like symptoms plus fever or nausea/vomiting point more strongly toward an infection, including a possible kidney infection [N2-R1][N2-R4]. By contrast, chronic pelvic pain, pressure, and urgency without fever or blood in the urine are more suggestive of IC or OAB [N1-F1][N1-R3][N6-R1]. The evidence also notes that bladder cancer can present with similar symptoms, including pain when urinating, urgency, frequent urination, and pain, but it usually has the main warning sign of painless blood in the urine, and the evidence explicitly says that the main warning sign of bladder cancer is painless gross hematuria [N2-R2][N4-R2]. So if you have painless blood in the urine, that should raise concern for bladder cancer, even though it may look like other conditions [N2-R2].

In short, the most likely causes are UTI, IC, OAB, and possibly kidney infection or bladder cancer [N1-F1][N1-R3][N6-R2][N2-F2]. Infection-related causes are more likely to be accompanied by fever, chills, nausea/vomiting, flank pain, or blood in the urine, whereas noninfectious causes like IC or OAB are more likely to be chronic with persistent urgency and pain without clear infection signs [N2-R1][N2-R4][N1-F1][N1-R3]. **Should you be worried about bladder pain and frequent urination?**

Yes, it’s reasonable to be concerned, but not always alarming. The evidence points to several common causes, and the main question is whether your symptoms are mild and short-term or more serious and urgent [N7][N8]. The most likely explanations are **urinary tract infection (UTI)**, **interstitial cystitis (IC)/bladder pain syndrome**, **overactive bladder (OAB)**, and less commonly **kidney infection** or **bladder cancer** [N7][N8][N9]. The key difference is whether your symptoms are infection-related or noninfectious, and whether they include red flags like fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, flank pain, or blood in the urine [N7][N8].

## 1) What is most likely happening?
### Common causes
- **UTI or bladder infection**: These are the most straightforward infection-related causes. They can cause **painful urination, frequent urination, burning, cloudy or smelly urine, and sometimes fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, or flank pain** [N2-R1][N2-R5][N2-R4][N7].  
- **Interstitial cystitis (IC)/bladder pain syndrome**: This is a **noninfectious chronic bladder condition**. It causes **bladder pain, pelvic pain, frequent urination, urgency, and sometimes nocturia**, but there is usually **no infection present** [N1-F1][N1-R3][N1-R4][N7].  
- **Overactive bladder (OAB)**: This is also noninfectious and is described as a **strong urge to urinate even when the bladder is not full**, with symptoms of **urinary urgency and frequent urination** [N6-R1][N6-R2][N7].  
- **Kidney infection**: This is a more serious infection that can develop from a bladder infection and may include **fever, chills, nausea/vomiting, flank or side pain, and blood in the urine** [N2-F2][N2-R4][N7].  
- **Bladder cancer**: While less common, it can present with similar symptoms such as **pain when urinating, urgency, frequent urination, and pain**, but it is most notable for **painless blood in the urine** [N2-R2][N4-R2][N7].

### Infection-related vs noninfectious
The main distinction is whether infection is likely.
